Okay, I'm going to start a journal.

As anyone who knows me would expect, it is going to be different than most. That's why I choose the name "Black Sheep". I am the "Black Sheep" of the Supply/Demand trading flock here at RTM.

If you are new to Supply/Demand trading, I urge you to read the wonderful journal here like. I wont mention any names simply because I do not want to leave any out. Which is another way of saying you can't go wrong with any of them. My journal is different.

I am going to attempt to do two things:

(1) Show open Supply/Demand Delta Zones on various 60 minute (or higher) charts. These zones are not trade signals (more on this later). (2) Show trades taken on the 5 minute time frame for the EUR/USD and JPY/USD currencies. These trades will primarily be shown in hindsight, but I will include information from my trading station for verification. If you saw my old journal at FF, then you know what I mean.

Here are two recent charts of Gold (XAU/USD cdf). BTW as an American, I can not trade this cdf. I could of course trade the futures contract, but I would never do that on such a large time frame which could mean holding overnight.

Again, no prognostications are being made here. We simply see open Supply or Demand Zones. These Zones are ideal places to look for either shorts or longs respectively. I believe that these zones are not trade signals in and of themselves. Therefore, I need to see some type of entry signal within them to get into the market. That is why another name for these zones is Entry Signal Zone.

The basis for my zones is the concept of AGGRESSION. I want to get into that concept in the next post.

author: HiddenGap
text:
A lot of well meaning people often make a huge mistake when trying to explain why the market did what it did at any given time. They say things like, " the market went up today because there were more buyers than sellers". Or they say," the market went down due to a 'seller's' strike". These are completely wrong. The market's sole purpose is to bring a buyer and a seller together. Every price where a transaction takes place MUST have a buyer and a seller.

WHAT MOVES THE MARKETS, IS THE RELATIVE ENTHUSIASM OR AGGRESSION OF EITHER THE BUYER(S) OR THE SELLER(S).

Let's take a simplified example.

Suppose you want to buy a car. The price you are willing to pay is 50,000. The seller of the car is asking for 100,000. Now let's suppose we can't just split the difference and make a transaction at 75,000.

The car will sit there and no transaction will happen unless one of you is willing to move. Suppose you as a buyer see three more potential buyers coming. You may now have incentive to raise your price to 100,000. You are now willing to hit the ASK. This willingness is enthusiasm or aggression. The opposite could be true as well. Suppose the Seller becomes aware that another sellers of the same car is coming and is willing to take 45,000. The first seller would have incentive to quickly lower his price to 50,000. That is, the seller needs to hit the BID and make a transaction happen before the buyers gets word of the other car on the market.

This is what actually moves the market. Buyers willingly hitting the ASK will raise price and Sellers willingly hitting the BID will cause price to fall. Therefore, If we want to determine where a key change in the supply/demand dynamic as taken place, we look for where the sellers have been more aggressive (hitting the BID), which we call supply. Or we look for where the buyers have been more aggressive (hitting the ASK), which we call demand.

There are a few more things that go into the definition of an Aggression bar. The main point is that for every buyer there is a seller. A transaction takes place when one side moves aggressively to accept the price from the other.

author: HiddenGap
text:
So, how do we interpret aggression on a price chart?

There are some basic elements we are looking at:

(1) Volume

(2) Range (3) Effort (4) MidPoint trend (5) Open/Close percentages (6) Hidden Gaps (7) Facilitation

" Green (+ tick volume and + MFI) A Green signifies three things:

1. More players are entering the market (+ volume); 2. The arriving players are biased in the direction the bar is moving; 3. The price movement is picking up speed as it goes (+ MFI)." Bill Williams

This is a key concept for understanding an aggression bar. We want to see a bar that has an increasing range on increasing volume. And we want to see volume proportional to the range.

Another very key factor is "MidPoint trend". If the midpoint of the current bar is greater than or equal to the high of the previous bar, the immediate trend is UP. If the midpoint of the current bar is less than or equal to the low of the previous bar, the immediate trend is DOWN. If buyers are being more aggressive than sellers, then one would expect to see the midpoint trend to be UP. If sellers are being more aggressive than buyers, then one would expect to see the midpoint trend to be DOWN.

We are also looking at volatility. We are measuring this in two ways. We are looking for candle bodies that are greater than the previous 3 intervals. Thus making the interval the largest candle body in 4 intervals (inclusive). This is the candle definition of a WRB, where B stands for body. We go one step further. We also look for the range to be the largest range (H-L) in 4 intervals (inclusive). This is the bar definition of a WRB, where B stands for bar.

To determine if an aggression bar is a key change in the supply/demand dynamic in the market, we will need to look at the price action following it. But before we do that, there is one element of the subsequent price action we need to see to determine if a true aggression bar occurred. All aggression bars form Hidden Gaps. Take a look at the chart above. Notice that the low of the candle after the "Climber" is greater than the high of the candle prior to the "Climber". This area is a Hidden Gap. If we were to erase the middle interval we would have an actual gap. We know actual gaps are valid supply/demand delta zones. These Hidden Gaps may be signaling a valid zone as well.

author: HiddenGap
text:
My last post to Romano83 got me thinking.

Actually, it brought up an issue that I have been struggling with for a long time: what is the best "Entry Signal Method" to use. In trading as in life, there are trade offs. No one method is perfect all the time.

Supply/Demand Zone trading seems to offer a unique situation with respect to entries. As I have stated before, I am not a "limit order" proponent. The main reason being I do not believe that a Supply or a Demand Zone is a trade signal in and of itself. I also believe this to be the case with Support and Resistance, which are not the same things as Supply and Demand.

Now I know that a the market can't always respect a zone (supply or demand), but it is the respecting of these zones that tends to give belief and trust in them. Yet, suppose the market respected the zones 90% of the time. However each time it did, it failed to give an entry signal. Where's the profit in that?

There are many times when the market respects my Supply/Demand Zones and no trade signal is given. This begs the question are the entry signal patterns lacking? Do I need less strict patters or more patterns in general? Although there are VSA patterns, I look at VSA as the alternative to a price pattern based entry signal. On the surface, VSA would seem to make more sense with Aggression Bars.

This is not a VSA thread, so I do not want to get too much into it. This is an example from Friday of the Yen.

Point A. is a wide spread down interval on increasing volume. However, note that the volume is less than average. The volume is also disproportionally small compared to the range of the interval. Of course note that this down interval is into an area where the buyers were previously aggressive.

Point B. is an Squat. The range of this interval is small than the previous interval, but the volume is greater. And although the interval makes a lower low than the previous interval it actually closes on its high. From a VSA perspective, this can only mean buying. This is a possible entry point. It's a bit "aggressive", but it tells the story you would want to hear. In an area where buyers were previously aggressive, we see increased activity( volume=activity) on an interval that is closing on the high after a wide spread down interval that was lacking in activity.

Point C. This is your basic No Supply. This down interval has volume less than the previous two intervals. In fact, it is colored grey because it is the lowest volume in the last 20 intervals. Volume is activity of the professional trader. Therefore if volume is this low, we can conclude that the professional traders are not interested in lower prices. If they are not interested in lower prices, it must be because they expect prices to rise. Again, buyers have already demonstrated that they were the more aggressive ones in area of the price chart. It should be of no surprise that as price falls back into this area the sellers are not aggressive and are in fact withdrawing.

Anyway, Point B is not a true hammer so I don't have a valid Hammer pattern for entry. None of the other patterns I look for are there either. So if I use VSA, I can get into this trade. If not, I can only take satisfaction in seeing the Supply/Demand Zone respected. Just seeing the Zone(s) respected is nice, but leaves your account the same. And lest I forget, there are certainly times when the VSA does not give an entry signal but a price pattern appears.

It's late and I am just rambling now. Forgive me. I would like to hear from some others who went through this struggle and how they came to reconcile it.

author: HiddenGap
text:
Once we have an Aggression bar that forms a hidden gap, we know we have a change in the Supply/Demand Dynamic in the market. However, not all changes are key changes. Only key changes in the Supply/Demand Dynamic become our Supply/Demand Zones.

In order to determine if a key change has occurred, we want to look at the price action following the appearance of the Aggression Bar. What we want to see is strong continuation. There are a couple of definitions of strong continuation. below is an example of one.

Notice that after the Aggression interval we see two consecutive white (close>open) that are making higher highs and not lower lows and are closing higher. Also not that both close higher than the close of the Aggression bar.

Basically, we are defining what Sam asks when he asks, "how does the market leave the (would-be) zone"?

author: HiddenGap
text:
Another example of the type of price action we want to see to confirm a key change in the Supply/Demand Dynamic has taken place involves Fractals. Fractal highs or lows are reaction points. They are also decision points.

If after the appearance of an Aggression bar, we see price move back into the range of the bar but fails to close the Hidden Gap before moving back out and forms a fractal, the market is telling us that this is in fact a Key change in the market.

Closing the Hidden Gap is very important. We never want to see price action close the HG prior to meeting a definiton that tells us a zone is created. Once the zone is created, the HG portion does not matter. A zone is open until price shows conviction above or below the zone..........

author: HiddenGap
text:
pres78 wrote: HG the bar before the one marked engulf fills the hidden gap. Does that now void this zone for you for any future trading?

Hello my friend.

The simple answer is no.

The Hidden Gap alerts us that there has been a change in the Supply/Demand Dynamic in the market. Once the market has shown that the change was KEY (via strong continuation for example) a Supply/Demand Zone is created. At this time, the Hidden Gap portion of the zone does not really matter much. Trade signals are valid as long as the Zone remains open.

There are some traders who only use the Hidden Gap as the Zone. If that were the case, this zone would still be valid for future trading because the interval that closed the Hidden Gap is involved in a valid trading pattern.

HiddenGap

Here's a good example of what the Hidden Gap can be telling us.

Notice in this example that we have a Drifter (interval where the aggression is by the sellers) that forms a hidden gap. We don't know if we have a KEY change in the Supply/Demand Dynamic, but we know we have had a change in it. We also note that the recent fractal low is within the range of the Hidden Gap. If the fractal low is some sort of decision point, then for this interval to be "gapping" through it must be of some importance.

Still, we don't know for sure until we see the subsequent price action. In this case we do get strong continuation. The definition of strong continuation in this case is, three dark (close<open) intervals with lower highs and lower lows closing lower than the close of the Aggression bar prior to then next swing. Where one of the three dark intervals is an Aggression bar that forms a Hidden Gap.

At the bottom we see an valid "fakie" long trade signal. It closes the gap but it does not close the zone. I like to see conviction to close a zone. Conviction would be a full (non doji) candle body below the zone, where said body's interval is not involved in a valid trade signal pattern.
